title: Building a Foundational Guardrail for General Agentic Systems via Synthetic Data
pdf_path: papers/Building a Foundational Guardrail for General Agentic Systems via Synthetic Data.pdf
threat_model_summary: An agent may produce a harmful action plan because of adversarial input or its own hallucination. A guardrail inspects the complete plan before execution and labels risk type and explanation. Evaluation uses synthetic and human-edited risk plans; no adaptive attacker targets the guardrail, and no executor is required to obey it.
core_contributions: AuraGen: a three-stage synthetic data engine for benign and risky agent trajectories
Safiron: an 8B pre-execution guardrail trained with SFT and GRPO
Pre-Exec Bench: 1,001 benign and 671 risky trajectories across eight risk categories
Safiron reaches 0.949 classification accuracy and 0.973 harmful recall
Case studies on MetaGPT and AutoGen with a log-format adapter
limitations: No adaptive attacker or evasion experiments
No executor enforcement; the guardrail is advisory, not a reference monitor
Plan-level only; runtime tool outputs and state changes are not inspected
Abstract's 'preserved task success' is not experimentally measured
'Harmful Detection Precision' is actually recall on risky samples; FPR/F1/AUROC are absent
Pre-Exec Bench labels leak into the SVM training-data filter, weakening the held-out claim
Benchmark keeps only unanimous human-approved samples, likely making it easier
No per-class or macro results; risk taxonomy categories overlap
Internal inconsistencies in data ratios, class accuracy, and RM splits
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
Risk classification is an empirical ML task, not a formal security property
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, OAuth, or capability tokens
Signed plan provenance and capability-gated execution are our inference; signatures authenticate the plan author, not plan safety
evidence_refs: pp.19-29 metric definitions, prompts, and human evaluation

title: When Agents "Misremember" Collectively: Exploring the Mandela Effect in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
pdf_path: papers/When Agents “Misremember” Collectively_Exploring the Mandela Effect in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: A subject agent answers a multiple-choice question after scripted group members provide misleading but plausible messages. The group is not independently misremembering; messages are generated to point at a target wrong answer. A long-term variant summarizes the conversation and later retrieves the summary. No external attacker or adaptive optimization is modeled.
core_contributions: MANBENCH: 20 BBH tasks, 4,838 multiple-choice questions, four domains, 13 models
Five protocols: baseline, generic/role-based groups, short/long-term memory
Error rate and reality-shift metrics (Err, sigma, sigma_max)
Documents answer flips under group pressure, e.g., GPT-5 17.63% to 41.59% and Llama3.1-8B 44.58% to 99.67%
Prompt-level defenses (Cognitive Anchoring, Source Scrutiny) and SFT resilience/cooperation training reduce sigma
limitations: 'Collective' is constructed: group agents are prompted to produce misleading text, and only one subject is measured
'Memory' is a natural-language summary, not a persistent memory system; summary faithfulness is not measured
No neutral-group or length-matched control; multi-agent context itself may drive part of the effect
No seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests
Influencer model/version/decoding parameters are unspecified
Prompt defenses confound role, structure, and output order
SFT only on two small models; no general-capability retention or held-out task test
No adaptive attacker against the defenses
Internal inconsistencies: GPT-5 GL below baseline, role-based exceptions beyond DeepSeek, unreproducible 74.40% average
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed message provenance and transparent logs are our inference; they authenticate who said something, not whether it is true
evidence_refs: pp.7-10 group size, scaling, defenses, limitations
pp.15-30 appendices with prompts, per-model tables, MedMCQA

title: PrivacyLens: Evaluating Privacy Norm Awareness of Language Models in Action
pdf_path: papers/PrivacyLens_Evaluating Privacy Norm Awareness of Language Models in Action.pdf
threat_model_summary: There is no malicious actor. An LM agent may unintentionally disclose sensitive information in a final communication action because it lacks contextual privacy norm awareness. The benchmark constructs vignettes and trajectories where sharing a sensitive item with the specified recipient is inappropriate.
core_contributions: PrivacyLens: 493 privacy-sensitive seeds, vignettes, and executable trajectories grounded in Contextual Integrity
1,479 probing questions at seed, vignette, and trajectory levels
Evaluates nine LMs on probing accuracy and action-level leakage (LR/LRh)
GPT-4 with a privacy-enhancing prompt reaches 98.99% probing but still leaks 24.54% (LR)/25.68% (LRh)
Documents a persistent knowing-but-not-acting gap
limitations: No attacker; only unintentional norm ignorance is studied
Evaluates only the final action, not intermediate tool calls or messages
One trajectory per seed; no worst-case search over instructions or observations
US-centric norms and a constructed binary 'should not share' label
No appropriate-sharing control set, so over-refusal can look private
LLM judge validated on 153 pairs; helpfulness agreement only kappa 0.56
LR aggregates any leaked item and ignores severity/quantity
Abstract reports LRh while calling it leak rate
theoretical_crypto_links: None; contextual privacy is a normative notion, not cryptographic privacy
No security game, theorem, proof, or reduction; LR is an LLM-judge rate
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, OAuth, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed relationship credentials and disclosure policies are our inference; they can bind who may receive what, but not whether disclosure is contextually appropriate
evidence_refs: pp.3-6 risk model, CI schema, benchmark construction
pp.7-9 main results and probing-action gap

title: Secret Collusion among AI Agents: Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography
pdf_path: papers/Secret Collusion among AI Agents_Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography.pdf
threat_model_summary: Two or more generative agents use steganographic covertext to coordinate or share secrets while an overseer reads the public channel. The DecAI model defines four overseer levels, from passive read access to state read/write. The overseer may be assumed able to decrypt, but this conflicts with the public-key steganography counterexample.
core_contributions: Defines and names secret collusion as multi-agent deception via steganography
DecAI system model with agents, multicast channel, knowledge, and four overseer capability levels
Ordinal incentive condition J(f_sc) > J(f) > J(f_c)
One grounding-function definition and four theorems/arguments: grounding detection, black-box optimization intractability, source-free randomness, and a paraphrase entropy bound
CASE benchmark of individual and group steganographic capabilities from GPT-2 to GPT-4
GPT-4 group covertext steganography succeeds 26%; standard ciphers such as Base64 reach 92% but AES standalone fails
Conceptual analysis of monitoring, paraphrasing, grounding, data filtering, and parameter optimization
limitations: Abstract claims a formal threat model and capacity insights, but there is no security game, advantage, KL/detection-error definition, or capacity theorem
Theorem 2 equates large/unknown common knowledge with intractability and has no reduction or complexity class
Theorem 3 assumes cryptographic hashing and neural-circuit feasibility; GPT-4 cannot compute SHA-256 correctly
Theorem 4 proves an upper bound on mutual information after paraphrasing, not subliminal-channel capacity
Overseer 'can decrypt' assumption conflicts with public-key steganography counterexample
Group evaluation gives A/B shared Wikipedia text but not the overseer, so 26% does not show equal-capability oversight failure
No N, confidence intervals, or statistical significance; no mitigation experiments
Real-world case is prompt-scaffolded and qualitative; 'perfectly secure' iMEC demo is a toy with a fixed key
AES/SHA-256/OTP/public key appear only as capability targets, assumptions, or citations, not constructions
theoretical_crypto_links: No cryptographic security definition, game, reduction, or primitive construction
Information-theoretic steganography concepts (covertext, mutual information, entropy, Cachin/iMEC) are used, but the definitions are weak and there is no KL or detection-error bound
AES, SHA-256, OTP, and public-key steganography are capability targets or cited assumptions, not contributions
applied_crypto_links: Steganography and covert channels are the core applied-crypto-adjacent topic
No TEE, signatures, MACs, commitments, ZK, MPC, FHE, or key-management protocol
Shared-codebook key management and signed audit logs are our inference; they do not detect steganographic content
evidence_refs: pp.4-6 system model, steganography taxonomy, incentives
pp.7-8 CASE results and group evaluation
pp.22-48 appendices with proofs, prompts, and capability tables

title: AgentDAM: Privacy Leakage Evaluation for Autonomous Web Agents
pdf_path: papers/AgentDAM_Privacy Leakage Evaluation for Autonomous Web Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A benign setting with no malicious actor: an autonomous web agent may disclose task-irrelevant sensitive user facts in its actions. AgentDAM measures whether SENSITIVE_DATA appears in action text; prompt-based mitigations are evaluated. No prompt injection, malicious website, or adaptive attacker is modeled.
core_contributions: AgentDAM: 246 tasks across Reddit, Shopping, and GitLab in WebArena/VisualWebArena
Operationalizes data minimization as leakage of task-irrelevant SENSITIVE_DATA
End-to-end multi-step and multimodal web-agent evaluation with gpt-4o judge
Six agents show 9.8%-45.9% leakage without mitigation
Privacy-aware CoT raises privacy to 0.821-0.939 with 1.6-5.7 point utility loss
Task-level leakage drops from 162/246 to 73/246
limitations: Benign only; no external attacker or adversarial privacy attack
Single gpt-4o judge validated on one run with four humans
Per-action binary judgment; cross-action aggregation, hints, and anonymous-but-identifiable disclosures may be missed
Measures only task-irrelevant explicit disclosure, not relevant-but-unnecessary use
No error bars despite three-run averages
Only three web apps and eight task types
Prompt-level defense is not an execution boundary
Internal inconsistencies in privacy/leakage percentages and multimodal results
theoretical_crypto_links: None; data minimization is a semantic/normative property, not differential privacy or cryptographic privacy
No security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, OAuth, TEE, or capability tokens
Field-level capabilities and selective-disclosure credentials are our inference; they can restrict which fields are available, not whether disclosure is task-necessary
evidence_refs: pp.13-19 appendices with action space, data pipeline, judge prompt
